It feels like a fun challenge to build an engaging narrative from the start! Alright, let’s get going!

The seasonal treat-based countdown might these days have expanded into cosmetics and booze, but nothing beats 24 days of chocolate. At least, that’s what Lena told herself as she stood in the supermarket aisle, staring at a wall of advent calendars that ranged from budget foil to hand-painted wooden keepsakes. There were calendars promising tiny perfumes, artisanal gins, deluxe teas and even miniature scented candles, but she bypassed them with the stubborn loyalty of someone who knew precisely what December should taste like: cheap, slightly waxy milk chocolate that snapped too cleanly and melted too fast. Tradition, she thought, was not to be meddled with, even if it came wrapped in recyclable cardboard and social-media-ready illustration.

***

This article contains affiliate links to products. Our journalism is independent and is never written to promote these products although we may earn a small commission if a reader makes a purchase. The same couldn’t be said for Lena’s own life, which had begun to feel like one long, subtle advert for things she didn’t remember wanting. At twenty-nine, she ghost‑wrote “gift guides” for a lifestyle site whose editors spoke fluently in the language of clicks and conversions. All day she typed phrases like “you’ll wonder how you ever lived without it” about gadgets she would never buy, then turned off her laptop and went home to a one‑bed flat whose most extravagant feature was the good olive oil she only used when friends came over. Maybe, she thought, picking up a mid‑priced chocolate calendar with a cartoon fox on the front, what she needed was not more products, but better rituals.

***

On 1 December, she overslept, missed the gym, and opened door number one over the sink, still in her pyjamas. The chocolate behind it was a tiny bell, bent slightly at the edge where the mould had slipped. It tasted exactly as it always had: sweet, anonymous, the flavour of school discos and old lunchboxes. As she let it dissolve, she felt something quiet settle in her chest, like a small animal curling up to sleep. That evening, during a video call, her mother mentioned offhandedly that they still had the wooden advent calendar at home, the one Lena’s grandfather had carved—twenty-four lopsided drawers, each big enough for a marble or a wrapped sweet. “Your father filled it with screws last year,” her mum said, laughing. “Said he needed somewhere to keep them.” Lena thought of the cartoon fox calendar leaning on her kitchen counter and felt an unexpected surge of annoyance. Why, she wondered, had she left the real thing behind?

***

By the tenth, her days had fallen into a pattern: wake, open a cardboard door, eat a small chocolate, review yet another press release about the must‑have calendar of the season. There was one filled with mini skincare serums, another with tiny jars of jam. “It’s the idea of revealing something,” her editor said on their Monday call, “a little hit of surprise every morning. Comfort in uncertain times.” That afternoon, instead of filing the piece straight away, Lena opened a fresh document and began to write about the wooden calendar. She described the way her grandfather had sanded the edges and painted tiny scenes on the drawers—snowy hills, a crooked church, a robin that always looked slightly menacing. She remembered her father sneaking chocolate coins into the compartments when he thought no one was looking, and her younger self, waking in the dark to check that tomorrow’s drawer was still full, as if someone might have stolen the future overnight. Without planning to, she kept going, past her word count, past her deadline notification, until the article was less about calendars and more about the way time became bearable when it was broken into small, shared pieces.

***

The next day, her editor rang. “I can’t run this as a gift guide,” he said, “but I want it on the homepage as a column. We’ll put the usual affiliate boxes underneath, don’t worry.” To Lena’s surprise, she didn’t mind. For once, the products felt like an afterthought, trailing behind the story like children pulling sledges. The piece went live that afternoon, and by evening the comments were full of people describing their own advent rituals: hand‑drawn calendars made in kitchens, envelopes pinned to string, waxy chocolate eaten under duvets. Someone uploaded a photo of a wooden calendar almost identical to hers, screws and all. On 24 December, back at her parents’ house, Lena pulled open a familiar little drawer and found, beneath a curled wood shaving and a stray nail, a foil-wrapped chocolate coin. “Thought you might notice,” her father said, hovering in the doorway. Lena placed the coin on her tongue and let it melt, tasting not just sugar, but the slow, deliberate countdown of years that had brought her back to this room, this calendar, this moment. For the first time in a long time, the season felt less like an advert, and more like something you could step into and live.
